title: DRAM refinery re-bins decommissioned server DIMMs into CXL capacity
idea: First principle: DRAM has no intrinsic wear-out (no tunnel-oxide damage as in flash), so a 5-year-old server DIMM's cells are physically almost as good as new. Regional refineries pull retired DDR4/DDR5 at hyperscaler decommission, run 48-hour retention and pattern screens, re-bin at relaxed timing, and remount modules or dies onto CXL Type-3 expander cards for capacity-tier memory.
why: Usable supply and cost per bit: hyperscalers retire on the order of 10^8 GB/yr; recapturing ~30% adds several percent to global usable supply at ~10-20% of new-bit cost, with near-zero capital or scarce-resource intensity.

title: Per-row retention maps let controllers sell today's scrapped weak dies
idea: Leakage is a per-cell tail (<=13 fA), not a per-die property, yet dies that fail 64 ms retention in a few rows are fused down or scrapped. Ship such dies with an on-die retention map that a CXL/HBM controller reads to refresh only the weak rows at 8-16 ms, turning reject bins into saleable capacity.
why: Yield and cost per bit: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output that is now discarded; the extra refresh is confined to <1% of rows, so the energy penalty is negligible.

title: Data-lifetime-matched retention grade: short capacitors for AI working memory
idea: Retention only has to exceed the data's lifetime, and AI activations and KV-cache are rewritten every ~1-10 ms, not held for 64 ms. Define a JEDEC short-retention grade with a 4 ms guarantee; since required charge scales with leakage x hold time, Cs can drop ~40% (with shorter bitlines to keep Cs/Cbl), allowing AR ~30-35:1 capacitors built with fewer high-aspect-ratio etch and deposition steps.
why: Capacitor charge wall and capital: halving cylinder height removes the hardest HAR steps, lifts yield and frees etch-tool capacity; ~15-25% lower cost per bit for the AI tier.

title: EUV-free 1y-class DRAM micro-fab built from refurbished immersion scanners
idea: Derive the cost floor from tool $ per patterned layer: a 6F^2 cell at F~17 nm needs only 193i SAQP, and a refurbished immersion scanner costs ~1/8 of an EUV tool. Build a 10k-wafer/month U.S. line on second-hand 193i, etch and ALD tools running a frozen ~17 nm process, accepting ~50% of leading density at ~25% of capex per wafer start.
why: Capital intensity, EUV chokepoint and U.S. manufacturability: roughly 2x bits per capex dollar versus a leading-edge greenfield, and a 2-3 year ramp with no single-supplier tool.

title: Bit Purchase Agreements turn DRAM fabs into financeable infrastructure
idea: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so the cost of capital is a first-order term in $/bit. Copy the solar PPA: hyperscalers sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts for Gb/month at a fixed price, letting a new fab be project-financed largely with ~6-7% debt instead of a ~12-15% equity-weighted WACC.
why: Capital intensity and cost per bit: dropping WACC from ~13% to ~7% cuts the annualized capital charge ~30%, i.e. ~15% off cost per bit, and funds fabs that equity markets refuse at cycle peaks.

title: Cash-settled DRAM bit futures damp the cobweb shortage cycle
idea: The DRAM boom-bust behaves like a delay-line oscillator: a 3-5 year capacity lag chasing a ~1-year demand signal (cobweb model). A cash-settled Gb futures curve out to 4 years gives fabs a forward price to hedge expansions and buyers a way to lock supply, effectively shortening the control loop's delay.
why: Supply stability: lowers the peak-to-trough amplitude that produced the 4x price spike, and hedged revenue reduces risk premia on new capacity.

title: Strategic DRAM Die Reserve stored in dry-nitrogen vaults
idea: Unpowered, unpackaged known-good die hold no state and degrade negligibly in dry N2, so storage cost is essentially shelf space (<$0.01/GB-year). A government reserve buys die during gluts and releases them to domestic packagers during shortages, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
why: Supply resilience: a buffer of ~5% of annual demand flattens price spikes and counter-cycles the market at trivial carrying cost relative to fab capex.

title: Crucible-free Czochralski: pull 300 mm ingots from an induction cold-skull
idea: A crucible's only job is to contain molten silicon without contaminating it; a water-cooled segmented copper crucible with induction heating freezes a silicon skull that contains the melt in silicon itself. Adapt cold-crucible melting (used for Ti and nuclear glass) with magnetic melt stirring to CZ pulling, eliminating the high-purity quartz crucible.
why: Scarce resource: removes dependence on Spruce Pine (>80% of HPQ crucible quartz) and lowers interstitial oxygen; the risk is thermal-gradient control at 300 mm diameter.

title: Rack-level weight broadcast: one copy of model weights, many accelerators
idea: Information theory says N identical copies carry the information of one, yet inference clusters replicate the same weights in every accelerator's HBM. Put a single weight copy in a CXL/optical multicast memory appliance per rack and stream tiles with deterministic prefetch, keeping only working tiles and KV-cache in local HBM.
why: Do DRAM's job with less: for 8-64-way replicated serving, cuts weight-holding HBM 4-30x, freeing HBM wafer capacity (3x area/bit tax) at the cost of a few extra pJ/bit of streaming.

title: Microsecond memory exchange auctions stranded DRAM across tenants
idea: Measured cloud DRAM utilization averages ~50% because memory is provisioned per server for peak. A rack-scale CXL switch runs a continuous double auction that leases 256 MB segments between hosts with microsecond reassignment and hardware isolation, so idle bits are sold rather than stranded.
why: Usable supply: raising effective utilization from ~50% to ~75% is equivalent to ~50% more usable DRAM with zero new wafers.

title: Open DRAM reference PDK lets logic foundries enter commodity memory
idea: DRAM's moat is accumulated know-how, not physics: periphery is ~49% of the die and is ordinary CMOS. Fund an open reference design (cell, sense amp, redundancy, test) plus an open 1x-nm process recipe for licensed U.S. foundries, backed by an indemnified shared patent pool.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply diversity: lowers entry from ~$15B plus a decade of learning to a foundry add-on module, breaking the three-vendor oligopoly.

title: Array-only fabs: bond simple cell wafers to foundry-made periphery
idea: From first principles the array is a few periodic layers (wordline, bitline, capacitor) while periphery is generic logic. Split them: specialized array fabs with ~1/3 of a DRAM fab's tool set make cell wafers, logic foundries make periphery wafers, and wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding joins them (as CBA does for 3D NAND).
why: Capital and density: array-fab capex drops ~50%, die area per bit falls up to ~40% with periphery under the array, and each half runs on its optimal process.

title: Fab-in-a-factory: mass-produce identical modular DRAM fab bays
idea: Wright's law cuts cost ~20% per doubling, but every fab is bespoke construction built once. Design a standardized 2.5k-wafer/month fab module (cleanroom, sub-fab, utilities, tool set) prefabricated in a factory and shipped as ~40 truckable blocks, so each additional fab rides a learning curve.
why: Capital and time: after ~10 units construction cost falls ~50% and build time drops to 12-18 months versus 3-5 years.

title: Mask-free interference lithography for the periodic DRAM array layers
idea: A DRAM array is a periodic lattice whose information content is a few numbers (pitch, angle, phase); encoding it in a $1M mask and EUV photons is overkill. Expose the dense array layers with multi-beam 193 nm immersion interference or achromatic Talbot lithography, using a conventional scanner only for the cut, trim and array-edge layers.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital: removes 3-5 EUV layers with tools ~10x cheaper per layer; the risk is overlay of cut layers to the interference grating and edge defects.

title: Per-gigabit production tax credit rewards output, not buildings
idea: What the economy needs is good bits, so pay for bits: a $0.05-0.20/Gb credit for known-good DRAM made in the U.S., declining over 10 years, modeled on the wind production tax credit. Unlike capex grants it pays only for yield and utilization, forcing efficient operation.
why: U.S. manufacturability and cost: closes the ~25-40% U.S. cost gap at the margin and rewards yield, which capex grants ignore.

title: Buyer cooperative co-owns a fab and takes bits at cost
idea: Electricity co-ops proved users can own capital-heavy plants. OEMs, clouds and automakers buy equity in a memory co-op fab in proportion to their offtake and receive bits at cost-plus, removing the producer margin that balloons during shortages.
why: Cost per bit in shortages: members pay depreciation plus opex instead of 4x contract prices, and guaranteed offtake de-risks the financing.

title: Laser-decap and reball LPDDR die from discarded phones and laptops
idea: A GB of DRAM is ~42 mg of silicon whose value is entirely in its pattern, and discarded phones carry working LPDDR. Automated lines X-ray-locate PoP packages, laser-ablate mold compound, extract die, test them on a carrier, and rebuild them as fan-out packages for embedded, IoT and low-end PC markets.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2 billion phones/yr x 4-8 GB is several EB of DRAM entering e-waste (~20% of annual output); recovering 10% adds ~2% global supply with little capital.

title: Tool-level cryogenic helium recapture closes the fab helium loop
idea: Helium is never consumed chemically in a fab; it is simply vented. Fit each wafer-cooling and purge exhaust with a membrane plus cryo-adsorption recovery skid that recompresses and repurifies to 5N, reaching >90% recycle.
why: Scarce resource: cuts fab helium draw ~10x while Qatar (~30% of supply) is offline; payback under 2 years at current prices.

title: Ballroom-free fab: wafers travel only through sealed nitrogen tubes
idea: Particles kill yield only at the wafer surface, so cleanliness need exist only in the few liters around the wafer, not in a 10,000 m^2 class-1 ballroom. Connect tools with sealed N2-purged wafer conveyor tubes and FOUP-docked load ports so the building needs only gray-space HVAC.
why: Capital and energy: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and >40% of fab energy; removing the ballroom cuts both sharply.

title: Memory-as-a-lease with mandatory take-back keeps bits circulating
idea: Because DRAM bits do not wear out, transfer of ownership is the real waste mechanism. Manufacturers lease modules by GB-month with RFID-tracked serials and contractual take-back, then redeploy returned modules down a tier ladder (training to inference to enterprise to edge) over ~15 years.
why: Usable supply: triples service life per manufactured bit, multiplying cumulative supply ~2-3x for the same wafer starts.

title: Capacitorless gain-cell memory on idle U.S. 22-28 nm logic lines
idea: The charge wall is a capacitor problem; a 3T gain cell stores charge on a transistor gate and amplifies it locally, needing no special capacitor process. Run gain-cell memory dies on underused U.S. 22-28 nm FD-SOI logic lines, using reverse back-bias to push leakage down for ms-class retention, accepting ~3-4x DRAM cell area.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: zero new fab capex and immediate capacity for buffer and cache-tier memory from existing domestic lines.

title: Pay depreciated DRAM lines to keep running instead of converting
idea: A fully depreciated line's wafer cost is ~45% of a new one because depreciation is ~55% of cost. Governments or buyer consortia pay fabs to keep old 1x/1y-nm lines producing for 5 more years rather than converting them to HBM or scrapping tools, with guaranteed offtake covering the opportunity cost.
why: Cost per bit and supply: preserves the cheapest bits on Earth, adding ~10% supply at ~50% of new-node cost.

title: Pre-permitted fab-ready federal sites cut construction interest by a third
idea: Time is capital: on a $15B fab every year of construction costs ~$1B in interest and lost output. Pre-certify federal sites with completed environmental review, water recycling, 500 MW interconnects and gas lines so a fab can break ground in weeks and run in ~24 months.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-supply: shaves 1-2 years off the 3-5 year lead time and ~30% of interest during construction.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordline using all-TiN fill at sub-10 nm widths
idea: Below ~10 nm width, electron surface and grain-boundary scattering raise W's effective resistivity toward ~30-40 uOhm-cm while its barrier eats the cross-section; mean-free-path math shows a barrierless TiN or Ti-Al-N full fill lands within ~1.5x. Qualify a W-free buried wordline with all-TiN fill and a thin n+ poly-Si cap for work-function tuning.
why: Scarce resource: removes China-sourced tungsten (~80%) from DRAM's most W-intensive layer, at a small RC penalty offset by shorter wordline segments.

title: Chokepoint index printed per gigabit steers procurement off banned elements
idea: Compute each die's mass of every element per Gb, weight it by supply concentration (HHI) and geopolitical risk, and print an elemental chokepoint index on the datasheet. Federal and hyperscaler procurement scores bids on cost x (1 + index), so designs built only from Si, Al, Ti, Zr, Cu, O, N and C win.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: converts invisible supply risk into a price signal, pushing W, Co, Ru, Hf, Ta, In and Ga out within one product cycle.

title: Synthetic crucible silica from any beach sand via chloride distillation
idea: Purity is a chemistry problem, not geology: carbochlorinate ordinary sand to SiCl4, fractionally distill to 9N, flame-hydrolyze to fused silica soot, and form crucibles by slip casting plus arc fusion. Inputs are only Si, O, C, Cl and H.
why: Scarce resource: breaks Spruce Pine's >80% hold on HPQ crucibles, and fully synthetic walls lower metal contamination in ingots.

title: Zinc-silicon-oxide BEOL gain cells replace IGZO without indium or gallium
idea: Leakage physics depends on bandgap and trap density, not on indium: amorphous Zn-Si-O (~3.5 eV gap, with Si suppressing oxygen vacancies the way Ga does in IGZO) can give 2T0C gain cells with sub-1e-18 A off-current. Build them in the BEOL of any U.S. CMOS foundry, using only Zn, Si and O.
why: Refresh wall and scarce resource: In/Ga-free oxide memory with >100 s retention cuts refresh energy ~1000x and turns every logic fab into a potential memory fab.

title: Silicon-carbide access transistors make refresh-free DRAM in U.S. power fabs
idea: Junction and off-state leakage scale with intrinsic carrier density n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT); 4H-SiC (3.26 eV) has n_i ~1e-9 cm^-3, about 1e18 below Si, so retention moves from milliseconds to hours. Build 1T1C arrays on 200 mm SiC lines (already operating in the U.S.) using only SiC, SiO2, Al, Zr and TiN.
why: Refresh wall and U.S. manufacturability: eliminates refresh (16-33% of idle power) using domestic SiC capacity; risks are SiC/SiO2 interface traps, low channel mobility and ~3x wafer cost.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling gives a helium-free fab
idea: Gas-gap conductance in the molecular regime scales roughly with 1/sqrt(molecular mass), and H2's bulk conductivity (0.18 W/m-K) beats helium's (0.15); after accommodation-coefficient correction H2 lands within ~20%. Replace helium in electrostatic-chuck backside cooling and load-lock venting with electrolytic H2 at ~10 Torr in sub-milliliter volumes, diluted below flammability at exhaust.
why: Scarce resource: removes helium (with Qatar's ~30% offline) from etch and deposition tools using H2 made from water.

title: Supercritical CO2 cleaning slashes fab ultra-pure water demand
idea: Wet cleaning uses water only as solvent and particle carrier; supercritical CO2 (31 C, 74 bar) with alcohol cosolvent has near-zero surface tension, so it rinses high-aspect-ratio capacitor holes without pattern collapse. Replace most post-etch and pre-deposition wet rinses with closed-loop scCO2 recycled at >95%, using only C, O and H.
why: Water/energy and yield: cuts UPW use by >50% at fabs drawing ~10 ML/day and removes stiction-driven collapse of 60-75:1 pillars.

title: Eleven-element DRAM process built only from crustal commons
idea: Today's DRAM flow touches ~25 elements, each with its own gas cabinet, precursor chain and qualification. Restrict the whole flow to Si, O, N, H, C, B, P, Al, Ti, Zr and Cu (TiN electrodes, ZrO2/Al2O3 dielectric, poly-Si and TiN local wiring, Al/Cu interconnect), deleting whole classes of precursors and abatement systems.
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity: fewer gas lines, tools and suppliers, and a U.S. fab immune to every listed chokepoint.

title: Nanoimprint array patterning sidesteps EUV's ruthenium and molybdenum optics
idea: EUV mirrors rely on Mo/Si multilayers with Ru caps, so a Ru-free DRAM cannot lean on EUV. Pattern the periodic array layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from fused-silica (Si, O) replica templates cloned from one master, where pattern transfer costs mechanical contact rather than 92 eV photons.
why: EUV single-supplier and capital: NIL tools cost ~1/10 of EUV at ~1/10 the power, and array redundancy absorbs imprint defects.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly writes capacitor lattices with carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
idea: A symmetric diblock copolymer at its free-energy minimum forms hexagonal cylinders at a pitch set by chain length (~20-30 nm), exactly the storage-hole lattice. Guide PS-b-PMMA with a coarse DUV prepattern, harden it by sequential Al2O3 infiltration, and etch storage holes through the alumina mask.
why: Capital and EUV: replaces 1-2 EUV or SAQP layers with spin-coat and bake; defectivity must reach <0.01/cm^2 for full adoption.

title: Strontium-titanate capacitor on strontium-vanadate electrodes cuts aspect ratio threefold
idea: The charge wall says more charge needs k~70 or AR~115; thin-film SrTiO3 (k~150-300) clears it but historically needed Ru or Pt electrodes. Use SrVO3, a correlated-metal perovskite made of Sr, V and O, as a lattice-matched electrode to grow low-leakage STO at AR ~20:1.
why: Capacitor wall and capital: shorter capacitors remove the hardest HAR etch steps with no Ru; risks are small-gap leakage and crystallization thermal budget.

title: Cobalt-free manganese-nitride magnetic cells for refresh-free working memory
idea: Today's MTJs need Co, Ru, Ir and Pt; ferrimagnetic Mn4N has perpendicular anisotropy and low magnetization, and spin-transfer switching current scales with Ms x Hk. Build Mn4N/MgO/FeB tunnel junctions (Mn, N, Mg, O, Fe, B only) with no synthetic antiferromagnet, targeting ~10 ns switching and >1e15 endurance.
why: Refresh and scarce resources: nonvolatile DRAM-class memory on any logic BEOL with no listed elements; risks are TMR ratio and thermal stability at small sizes.

title: Repurpose idle LTPS display lines into silicon-only memory panels
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus >$10,000/m^2 for wafers; laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT gain cells at ~1 um rules, stacked 8-16 recrystallized layers deep on Gen-6 glass, can trade feature size for area cost. Build capacity-tier memory panels, diced into tiles, on idle LCD/LTPS lines using only Si, O, N, Al and Ti.
why: Capital and scarce resources: uses written-off display capacity with no EUV, HPQ crucibles or banned elements, targeting $/GB within ~2x of DRAM for capacity tiers.

title: Grow oxide memory arrays on cheap cast-silicon carriers, not prime wafers
idea: A BEOL oxide-TFT array needs only a flat, insulating, thermally stable carrier, not a dislocation-free crystal. Core 300 mm rounds from cast multicrystalline solar ingots, polish and oxidize them as carriers for Zn-Si-O memory stacks, then hybrid-bond onto a thin CMOS periphery wafer.
why: Scarce resource and cost: removes HPQ crucibles and CZ pulling from the array half of the die; carrier cost per wafer falls up to ~100x.

title: Vertical nanographite contacts replace tungsten and cobalt plugs
idea: In narrow plugs, metal resistivity is dominated by surface and grain-boundary scattering plus barrier volume, while vertically oriented graphene sheets conduct in-plane along the plug with no barrier. Grow carbon nanowall contacts by catalyst-free ~400 C PECVD inside contact holes and dope them by FeCl3 intercalation (Fe, Cl, C only).
why: Scarce resource: removes W and Co from bitline and storage-node contacts using limitless, domestic carbon; contact resistance at the TiN interface is the main risk.

title: Solder-free, indium-free HBM: copper hybrid bonds plus graphite heat spreaders
idea: A bond needs only atomic contact and Cu interdiffusion, so solder is a crutch: listed elements creep into HBM via indium TIM foils, SnAg bumps and Ta/Co barriers. Stack dies by Cu-Cu/SiCN hybrid bonding with TiN barriers and replace indium TIM with pyrolytic graphite sheets (~1500 W/m-K in plane).
why: HBM TSV tax and scarce resources: bumpless stacking cuts stack height and thermal resistance, raises yield by eliminating bump bridging, and removes In and Ta.

title: Open patent pool for abundant-element process substitutions
idea: Qualification cost scales with test-hours, not with the number of fabs, yet every fab re-qualifies substitutes alone and patents are scattered. A government-seeded pool licenses all abundant-element substitutions (TiN for W, ZrO2 for HfO2, Zn-Si-O for IGZO) FRAND at a flat per-wafer fee and publishes shared HTOL and retention data.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and U.S. manufacturability: shared reliability data cuts qualification time and cost, accelerating banned-element exit by years.

title: Sand-to-DRAM county campus with every input sourced domestically
idea: Transport and inventory buffers are pure overhead, so co-locate every abundant-element stage on one site: sand carbochlorination to SiCl4, polysilicon, synthetic-crucible ingots, wafers and an eleven-element DRAM fab, with Al, Ti and Zr precursors from domestic ilmenite and zircon sands. Cascade waste heat from polysilicon reactors into fab HVAC and water recycling.
why: U.S. manufacturability: zero foreign chokepoints for any input; inventory buffers and logistics risk collapse, and shared utilities cut capex.

title: Molten-salt electrolysis turns sand directly into polysilicon feedstock
idea: The thermodynamic minimum to reduce SiO2 is ~911 kJ/mol, yet carbothermic arc plus Siemens refining spends several times that. Electro-deoxidize SiO2 pellets in molten CaCl2 (FFC-style, ~850 C) to make silicon directly, then zone-refine, using only Si, O, Ca, Cl and C.
why: Scarce resource and U.S. manufacturability: modular plants break China's ~80% polysilicon share at potentially ~half the energy per kg.

title: Complementary Cu2O/ZnO oxide periphery lets entire memory live in BEOL
idea: Periphery (~49% of the die) is what pins memory to single-crystal silicon. Pair p-type Cu2O and n-type Zn-Si-O TFTs into low-temperature CMOS sense amps and decoders so both array and periphery deposit at <=400 C, allowing 10+ complete memory layers on any substrate.
why: Density and capital: monolithic 3D memory without 26-tier lateral Si transistors; the risk is Cu2O hole mobility (~1-5 cm^2/V-s) limiting periphery speed.

title: Insurance pricing rewards fabs that dual-qualify abundant substitutes
idea: Chokepoint disruption is a correlated, quantifiable loss. Business-interruption underwriters price premiums by each fab's banned-element mass dependency and discount fabs that hold pre-qualified abundant substitutes (TiN wordline, Zr-only dielectrics) able to switch within 90 days.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: aligns private capital with resilience; premium savings pay back qualification costs in ~3 years.

title: Protonic double-layer storage node packs tenfold charge per area
idea: The charge wall assumes a dielectric; an electric double layer (Debye length ~1 nm) stores ~10-20 uF/cm^2, ~10x a ZrO2/Al2O3 stack. Fill a shallow storage node with a hydrated nanoporous silica proton conductor between TiN electrodes so a planar or AR ~10:1 cell holds ~5 fF, with proton hops charging in nanoseconds.
why: Capacitor wall and capital: removes high-aspect-ratio etch and deposition tools, the biggest fab cost driver; charging speed and faradaic leakage are unproven.

title: Hafnium-free periphery transistors with zirconium-silicate gate dielectrics
idea: DRAM periphery needs EOT ~1.2-1.5 nm, not logic's ~0.8 nm, so HfO2's k~25 is overkill: ZrSiOx (k~12-18) or ZrO2/SiON with TiN gates meets the leakage spec. Qualify a Hf-free periphery high-k metal-gate module fed from widely mined zircon (ZrSiO4).
why: Scarce resource: removes Hf, a by-product with very few refiners, from the periphery at minor performance cost.
